title: IAM Roles, STS & Cross-Account Access
summary: Temporary credentials for workloads, other accounts, third parties and on-premises servers.
tldr: Whenever an answer stores long-term access keys, look for the **role** alternative: instance profile, Lambda execution role, task role, Pod Identity, Roles Anywhere or a cross-account role.
Cross-account access works two ways: **assume a role** in the other account, or call a resource that has a **resource-based policy** naming your principal. Both sides must allow it.
Third-party SaaS access uses a role that trusts the vendor's account **plus an `sts:ExternalId` condition** to prevent the confused-deputy problem.

keyFacts.text: A role's maximum session duration can be set between 1 and 12 hours. Chained role sessions (role assuming a role) are capped at 1 hour.
A secret-ish value unique per customer in the trust policy. It stops another customer of the same vendor from tricking the vendor into using your role.
**IAM Roles Anywhere** exchanges a certificate from your trusted CA (trust anchor) for temporary STS credentials on servers outside AWS.
Session-token metadata requests (`HttpTokens=required`) block SSRF attacks that steal instance role credentials through IMDSv1.
When a service principal (s3, sns, events) invokes your Lambda, add `aws:SourceArn` and `aws:SourceAccount` so only that exact resource can call it.

keywords.answer: Lambda resource policy with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount

keywords.cue: all accounts in the org, including future ones, may pull
role may be assumed only with MFA
keywords.answer: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent true in the role trust policy

traps: Giving a vendor IAM user access keys, even encrypted or rotated, is never the secure answer.
Requiring MFA on the trust policy does not solve the confused-deputy problem; the external ID does.
Adding permissions to the EKS node instance role gives them to **every** pod on that node.
A cross-account resource policy alone is not enough: the caller's own account must also allow the action in an identity policy.
Raising the IMDS hop limit so pods can use the node's credentials is the opposite of least privilege.
